references.text: Abram builds an altar to the Lord after the revelation at Shechem and calls on the name of the Lord at Bethel—a parallel to the patriarchs' practice of building altars and worshiping.
Abram builds an altar to the Lord by the oaks of Mamre in Hebron, demonstrating the patriarchs' repeated practice of building altars and worshiping the Lord.
The earliest mention of calling on the name of the Lord, which Isaac also does when he builds an altar at Be'er-Sheba.
Abraham plants a tamarisk tree in Be'er-Sheba and calls on the name of the Lord there—a direct precursor to Isaac's altar-building and worship at the same place.
God instructs Jacob to go to Bethel and build an altar, consistent with the patriarchal tradition of building altars at places where God has revealed Himself.
The Lord reveals Himself to Isaac during the night and gives him promises, which is the direct occasion for Isaac to build an altar and call on the name of the Lord.
Isaac's actions in Gerar mirror Abraham's early journey and confirm the continuity of God's promise through successive generations.
Isaac restores Abraham's altar at the same place, showing continuity in God's revelation and the faith of the patriarchs.
Both patriarchs mark their encounter with God by building an altar and giving the site theological significance after a conflict.
Contrasting altar actions: Abraham's burnt offering altar on Moriah versus Isaac's peace offering altar in Gerar show God's guidance in both testing and blessing.
Strong parallel: Both verses directly link the building of an altar and calling on the name of the Lord with a clear divine response.
